results.text: Identifies ERISA section 724 (29 U.S.C. 1185m), enacted by section 201 of Division BB of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021, as the provision that governs Halvorsen's self-funded ERISA plan (references to the parallel PHSA 2799A-9 / IRC 9824 provisions are acceptable in addition, but a memo that relies only on the PHSA or on "the No Surprises Act" without identifying the ERISA provision fails).
results.rationale: The memo identifies ERISA § 724 (29 U.S.C. § 1185m) as the governing provision for the self-funded ERISA plan and cites the PHSA/IRC parallels as additional authority. It does not rely only on the PHSA or describe the law merely as the No Surprises Act.
results.evidence: "In our view the Meridian Administrative Services Agreement ("ASA") contains several provisions that ERISA § 724 (29 U.S.C. § 1185m), the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 ("CAA") gag clause prohibition, does not allow." ... "ERISA § 724(a)(1) (parallel provisions: PHSA § 2799A-9 and IRC § 9824) provides that a group health plan 'may not enter into an agreement'..."

results.text: Concludes that Section 9.4's requirement of Meridian's prior written consent before the Plan shares claims data with consultants or auditors is a prohibited restriction under section 724(a)(1)(C) on sharing data with, or directing that data be shared with, a business associate.
results.rationale: The memo squarely concludes § 9.4's consent requirement is a prohibited restriction under § 724(a)(1)(C) as applied to business associates, with high confidence, not merely 'problematic'.
results.evidence: "Section 724(a)(1)(C) protects the plan's right to share (A)/(B) data, 'or direct[] that such data be shared', with a HIPAA business associate. Consultants, actuaries, auditors and successor TPAs are the classic plan business associates. A clause that requires Meridian's consent, and lets Meridian define the permitted purpose, is a direct restriction on exactly that." Heading: "Section 9.4: Third-party recipients and the 'Competitor' definition (prohibited as applied to business associates; high confidence)"

results.text: Concludes that Section 9.5's bar on the Plan Sponsor disclosing provider-specific reimbursement rates, allowed amounts, or provider quality ratings to participants, network providers, or referring providers is prohibited by section 724(a)(1)(A).
results.rationale: The memo concludes § 9.5's bar on disclosing rates, allowed amounts and quality ratings to participants, network providers and referring providers is prohibited by § 724(a)(1)(A), and rejects the member-portal sentence as a cure.
results.evidence: "Section 9.5: Provider rate confidentiality (prohibited; high confidence)... This is close to a word-for-word mirror of what § 724(a)(1)(A) forbids." ... "The last sentence does not cure the problem... The statute protects the plan's freedom to share by 'any other means', not just through Meridian's tool."

results.text: Explains that the section 724(a)(2) exception for "reasonable restrictions on the public disclosure" applies only to the provider-specific cost and quality information described in paragraph (1)(A) and therefore cannot be used to justify restrictions on access to or sharing of de-identified claims data under (1)(B) or (1)(C).
results.rationale: The memo states the (a)(2) exception is limited to (1)(A) information and expressly draws the consequence that nothing comparable limits (B) or (C); it also notes the 'public' portion of § 9.5 may be preserved.
results.evidence: "Section 724(a)(2) allows 'reasonable restrictions on the public disclosure' of information, but only the paragraph (1)(A) information. Nothing comparable limits (B) or (C)." ... "The ban on public disclosure is the one part of § 9.5 that § 724(a)(2) permits, if reasonable."

results.text: Concludes that Section 9.6's audit limits (once per plan year, a sample capped at 250 claims selected by Meridian's methodology, on Meridian's premises or a view-only portal) are impermissible restrictions on electronic access to de-identified claims data, not merely commercially unfavorable terms.
results.rationale: The memo concludes that § 9.6's 250-claim cap, Meridian-selected sample, view-only/portal review and pricing-field limits operate as a restriction under § 724(a)(1)(B) and (C) as applied to the Plan's auditor, distinguishing them from genuinely commercial terms about access to Meridian's internal systems. The conclusion is hedged ('to the extent') and does not separately classify the once-per-year limit, but it reaches the required conclusion that the data-limiting audit caps are prohibited restrictions, not merely unfavorable commercial terms.
results.evidence: "Where it is a gag clause... Meridian is using § 9.6 to limit the electronic claim-level data the Plan's auditor (a business associate) may receive: view-only review, 250 claims, and 'claim-level pricing fields' only through a separate priced engagement. To that extent, § 9.6 operates as a restriction under § 724(a)(1)(B) and (C)." Table: "§ 9.6: audit limited to 250 claims, Meridian's sampling, view-only portal, non-'Competitor' auditor... A gag clause to the extent it limits giving claim-level data to the Plan's auditor (a business associate)."

results.text: Acknowledges that section 724 and the Departments' guidance do not prescribe a required format, delivery mechanism, turnaround time, or price for electronic access, and accordingly frames the fee, 180-day lag, and standard-format terms of Section 9.3 as a question of whether they "directly or indirectly restrict" access rather than asserting that any fee or delay is a per se violation.
results.rationale: The memo explicitly acknowledges the statute is silent on format, frequency, turnaround and price, declines to treat any fee or delay as per se unlawful, and analyzes § 9.3 under the 'directly or indirectly restrict' standard.
results.evidence: "Mr. Delacroix is correct that § 724 does not expressly regulate format, frequency, turnaround or price. But the statute reaches agreements that restrict access 'directly or indirectly'." ... "A court or agency could reasonably conclude that a modest, cost-based charge and a reasonable delivery period are permissible. We would not advise the Committee that every fee is unlawful."

results.text: Concludes that the Section 9.3 terms, taken together (claim-level allowed amounts and provider identifiers available only as a paid "custom extract" at $18,500 plus $0.11 per line, a 180-day delivery window running from an acceptance for which there is no deadline, and Meridian's right to decline extracts that would reveal "Proprietary Information"), operate as an indirect restriction on per-claim access to the data elements section 724(a)(1)(B) expressly lists, and are therefore likely prohibited.
results.rationale: The memo concludes the § 9.3 structure (fee on enumerated fields, 180-day lag from an acceptance with no deadline, decline right tied to 'Proprietary Information' including allowed amounts) operates as an indirect restriction on the per-claim elements listed in (a)(1)(B), and rejects the standard extract as satisfying (B).
results.evidence: "A standard extract built specifically to leave out the enumerated elements does not discharge the obligation. Moving those elements behind a fee-and-discretion gate is a restriction." ... "No real deadline. Delivery is 180 days after Meridian's 'written acceptance', and there is no deadline for acceptance... a pricing and timing structure that, combined with the decline right, can delay or deny the statutory data indefinitely is in our view an indirect restriction."

results.text: States that Meridian's classification of allowed amounts and provider-specific rates as "Meridian Proprietary Information" cannot override section 724, because the statute expressly lists allowed amounts and provider name and clinical designation among the per-claim elements the Plan must be able to access.
results.rationale: The memo connects Meridian's 'proprietary' label to the statutory enumeration of allowed amount and provider name/clinical designation and rejects it, also citing Transparency in Coverage publication.
results.evidence: "Meridian has contractual discretion to refuse the very data elements § 724(a)(1)(B)(i) and (ii) name: 'the allowed amount' and provider 'name and clinical designation'." ... Response table: "'Allowed amounts are proprietary' | The statute names the allowed amount; Transparency in Coverage files already publish negotiated rates; reasonable confidentiality protects any residual interest."

results.text: Correctly explains that "de-identified" in section 724(a)(1)(B) refers to removal of participant and beneficiary identifiers under the HIPAA de-identification standard (45 C.F.R. 164.514), and does not suggest that provider identities, provider NPIs, or provider-level pricing must or may be removed to make the data "de-identified."
results.rationale: The memo correctly describes de-identification under HIPAA § 164.514 (safe harbor/expert determination) as concerning individual identifiers and expressly states provider NPIs and names are not patient identifiers and need not be removed.
results.evidence: "Under the HIPAA safe harbor (45 C.F.R. § 164.514(b)(2)), all date elements other than year that relate to an individual must be removed... (Provider NPIs and names are not patient identifiers and need not be removed. A consistent de-identified member key is permissible if it meets § 164.514(c).)"

results.text: Explains that section 724 is directed at the Plan (the Plan "may not enter into" an agreement containing such restrictions) so that compliance and attestation exposure rests with the Plan and its fiduciaries regardless of who drafted the ASA or what Meridian's compliance team has represented, and does not describe Meridian as the party that is itself in violation of section 724.
results.rationale: The memo places the § 724 obligation on the Plan and its fiduciaries regardless of Meridian's representations, and does not describe Meridian as itself violating § 724; it treats Meridian's exposure as contractual/reputational.
results.evidence: "The prohibition binds the plan: it is the plan that 'may not enter into' the agreement. Meridian is squarely within the class of counterparties covered." ... "Remedies directly against Meridian under ERISA § 502(a)(3) are uncertain: § 724 binds the plan, and Meridian is a fiduciary only for claims decisions. Contract remedies under § 9.7 and the BAA are the more reliable route."

results.text: Advises that the Section 9.7 compliance-with-law savings clause does not cure the prohibited provisions for attestation purposes, and recommends that the offending language be amended or deleted rather than relying on Section 9.7.
results.rationale: The memo rejects Meridian's 'by definition' argument with multiple reasons (court/agency trigger, provisions remain operative and are being applied, covers only 'access') and recommends amending/deleting the offending provisions.
results.evidence: "The second sentence works only after a court or agency rules... Until then the provision stays in force." ... "Meridian is not applying § 9.7 as a rule of construction... Its conduct shows the specific provisions control in practice." ... "The must-haves are: delete the decline right; ... § 9.5 limited to public disclosure..."

results.text: Flags that the December 2024 and December 2025 attestations were submitted as unqualified "in compliance" attestations while Article 9 was in force, identifies this as a compliance exposure for the Plan, and recommends a documented remediation approach for the prior attestations (for example documenting the reliance on Meridian's confirmation, correcting the record with the Departments or in the next attestation's Additional Information field, and preserving a remediation file).
results.rationale: The memo flags the 2024 and 2025 unqualified attestations as very likely inaccurate, assesses the exposure, and recommends a concrete remediation path (document reliance, confirm with CMS whether correction is possible, disclose in 2026 Additional Information, preserve evidence) without asserting a formal amendment mechanism definitely exists.
results.evidence: "Given our Part IV conclusions, both attestations were very likely inaccurate. Exposure, which we assess as low to moderate if addressed promptly..." ... "Document the good-faith reliance record now... Correct the record. First, confirm with CMS... whether a prior-period attestation can be amended or resubmitted... In any event, use the 2026 attestation's Additional Information field to disclose..."

results.text: Advises that Halvorsen must still submit the attestation due December 31, 2026 and, if Meridian has not amended Article 9 by then, must disclose the non-compliant provisions and the steps taken to remove them in the attestation's "Additional Information" field, consistent with the Departments' FAQ guidance, rather than skipping the attestation or attesting unqualified compliance.
results.rationale: The memo insists the Plan must file by December 31, 2026, must not attest unqualified compliance, and must disclose the provisions and remediation steps in Additional Information if Meridian has not fixed the contract.
results.evidence: "The Plan must file. Failing to file is a separate violation and would look worse than a qualified filing." ... "Meridian refuses or stalls | File the attestation identifying noncompliance (or attest with an explanation...). Describe the provisions, the Plan's written demand for removal, Meridian's refusal, and the Plan's next steps." ... "Never file an unqualified 'in compliance' attestation for 2026 on the current record."

results.text: Recommends that the Plan put HIPAA business associate agreements in place with Northgate and Claimsight (or confirm their business associate status) and direct Meridian to furnish the de-identified data to them, and concludes that Meridian cannot rely on the "Competitor" definition or its consent right in Section 9.4 to block sharing with a business associate.
results.rationale: The memo recommends confirming Plan BAAs with Northgate and Claimsight, directing data to them as business associates, and concludes Meridian cannot use the Competitor definition or § 9.4 consent right to block sharing, while allowing reasonable confidentiality terms.
results.evidence: "Can Meridian block Northgate as a 'Competitor'? No, not lawfully as to the § 724 data, provided Northgate receives it as the Plan's business associate." ... "Designate Northgate and Claimsight as Plan business associates receiving the data on the Plan's behalf. Confirm both have signed Plan BAAs..." ... "What Meridian can legitimately ask for: reasonable confidentiality, use-limitation and data-security undertakings..."

results.text: Proposes amendment terms for Article 9 that (a) delete the consent requirement for sharing with the Plan's business associates and (b) specify the per-claim data elements to be furnished, expressly including allowed amounts and provider names or identifiers.
results.rationale: Appendix A deletes Meridian's consent over sharing with Plan business associates (replaced by BAA plus confidentiality undertaking) and specifies per-claim elements including allowed amounts and provider name/NPI.
results.evidence: "§ 9.4... 'The Plan may share, and may direct Meridian to share, Claims Data and Standard Reports with any Business Associate of the Plan upon written notice to Meridian... Meridian's consent shall not be required'" ... "§ 9.3(a)... de-identified Claims Data for each Participant, including Allowed Amounts and other claim-related financial information, provider name, NPI and clinical designation, service codes..."

results.text: Proposes amendment terms that address timing and cost of data access, by specifying a defined reasonable delivery timeframe for claim-level extracts and limiting any charge to a reasonable cost-based fee (or no fee for standard electronic access).
results.rationale: The proposed amendment sets specific acceptance and delivery deadlines and limits fees to no charge for the statutory feed and a capped, documented cost for bespoke work.
results.evidence: "(c) Meridian shall confirm each request in writing within ten (10) business days and deliver historical extracts within thirty (30) days..." ... "(e) Meridian may charge its reasonable, documented cost for custom analytics or formats beyond (b), not to exceed $[cap] per request, but no fee shall apply to data described in (a)."

results.text: Recommends that the amendment require Meridian to represent that none of its downstream agreements (including Meridian Choice network provider contracts) restricts the Plan's rights under section 724, or otherwise addresses the risk that a downstream Meridian agreement could indirectly restrict the Plan.
results.rationale: The memo flags that Meridian's provider network agreements could flow restrictions through to the Plan and proposes a representation, warranty, certification and indemnity covering them.
results.evidence: "Meridian's 2024 email also represented that its provider network agreements contain no gag clauses. We have not seen them... restrictions in them could flow through to the Plan's access. The amendment should include a representation and indemnity covering them." ... "Meridian represents and warrants that this Agreement and its Network Provider agreements comply with ERISA § 724..."

results.text: Connects the data request to the Committee's ERISA fiduciary duties, explaining that the duty to prudently select and monitor service providers and to ensure plan expenses are reasonable supports obtaining the claims data, and recommends that the Committee document its efforts.
results.rationale: The memo frames the data request in terms of the Committee's duty to monitor service providers and ensure fee reasonableness and recommends documenting the process in minutes.
results.evidence: "Duty to monitor and fee reasonableness. The Committee oversees about $71 million in claims and $2.1 million in fees and has never independently verified network pricing. Getting the data, benchmarking, and auditing are the right steps. The Committee's minutes should document its process: the reasons, the advice received, and the decisions made."

results.text: Identifies potential excise tax exposure under Internal Revenue Code section 4980D ($100 per day per affected individual) for a group health plan's failure to satisfy the Code's parallel gag clause provision (IRC 9824), as part of the Plan Sponsor's exposure analysis.
results.rationale: The memo identifies IRC § 4980D excise tax exposure ($100/day/affected individual) for a § 9824 failure, Form 8928 self-reporting, and the reasonable-cause mitigants, while flagging the uncertainty.
results.evidence: "IRC § 9824 is enforced through the § 4980D excise tax: $100 per day per affected individual, subject to self-reporting on Form 8928. How § 4980D applies to a gag clause is genuinely unclear..."

results.text: Notes that the 90-day non-renewal notice deadline under Section 12.1 (October 2, 2026) has passed, so the ASA will renew for calendar 2027, and factors this into the recommended negotiating approach (for example relying on Meridian's exposure to a reported gag clause and the Plan's fiduciary posture rather than on a non-renewal threat, or considering Section 12.2 breach-based termination).
results.rationale: The memo notes the October 2, 2026 deadline has passed, the ASA renews through 2027, and recalibrates leverage to the statute, § 9.7, the BAA, Meridian's 2024 assurance, § 12.2 breach termination, and a 2028 RFP rather than a non-renewal threat.
results.evidence: "The October 2, 2026 non-renewal deadline has passed. The ASA renews automatically for calendar 2027... Halvorsen's commercial leverage is therefore weaker in the short term, but its legal leverage is strong: the statute itself, and Meridian's own § 9.7; BAA §§ 3.2 and 9.1; Meridian's 2024 written assurance...; the § 12.2 termination-for-cause right; a credible 2028 RFP."

results.text: Relies on the Section 12.4 "Changes in Law" clause as the mechanism that obligates Meridian to amend the ASA, even though section 724 was enacted in December 2020 and is not a change in law enacted after the January 1, 2024 Effective Date.
results.rationale: Negative criterion avoided: the memo does not invoke § 12.4 as the lever and expressly explains why it does not apply because the CAA predates the Effective Date.
results.evidence: "Section 12.4 provides no cost-recovery hook... The CAA was enacted December 27, 2020, three years before the January 1, 2024 Effective Date, so § 12.4 does not apply."

results.text: Is formatted as a memorandum addressed to Dana Okafor and opens with an executive summary that states the bottom-line conclusions before the detailed analysis.
results.rationale: The deliverable is a memorandum addressed to Dana Okafor with a 'Bottom line' executive summary at the top preceding the detailed analysis.
results.evidence: "**To:** Dana Okafor, General Counsel, Halvorsen Industrial Group, Inc." ... "## I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY — Bottom line. In our view the Meridian Administrative Services Agreement ('ASA') contains several provisions that ERISA § 724... does not allow."
